### HTML scraping

Does including header content improve predictions? Answer the question and provide quantitative evidence supporting your answer.

## Preliminary Task 1

We briefly considered whether header information meant including each page's `<h1>`–`<h6>` tags, or if that was referring instead to the `<head>` tag. Because of this confusion, we opted to run our PCA and Logistic Regression models on three parse functions: the first of which only included `<p>`, the second including both `<h1>`–`<h6>` and `<p>`, and the third which included `<head>` and `<p>`. We found that the best model included both `<h1>`–`<h6>` and `<p>` tags, achieving **74.6% accuracy**, compared with **73.5% accuracy** for the model using only `<p>` tags, an improvement of **1.1 percentage points**. The model including `<head>` and `<p>` tags achieved the worst score, with **60.7% accuracy**. These results suggest that including header information improved predictive performance under our updated preprocessing approach.

### Bigrams

Do bigrams capture additional information relevant to the classification of interest? Answer the question, **briefly** describe what analysis you conducted to arrive at your answer, and provide quantitative evidence supporting your answer.

### Preliminary Task 2: Bigram Analysis

We investigated whether including bigrams (two-word combinations) improved binary webpage classification compared with using individual words alone. Using our shared preprocessing script, we converted cleaned webpage text into numerical features using TF-IDF and applied PCA to reduce the number of variables. We then fitted logistic regression models using word-based predictions, with and without additional bigram principal components. The word-only model achieved **56.4% accuracy** on 429 validation webpages, compared with **64.8% accuracy** for the model incorporating bigrams, an improvement of **8.39 percentage points**. Adding bigrams changed 76 individual predictions and improved performance above the majority-class baseline of 52.4%. These results suggest that bigrams provided additional predictive value under our updated preprocessing approach. However, several common bigrams contained webpage formatting terms rather than meaningful text, suggesting that further cleaning may improve model performance and interpretability.
